title: Deeds without measure (Mishnah Peah 1:1)
hook: the morning service lists things with no limit: honoring parents, kindness, hospitality, visiting the sick

segments.voice: Yesterday, neshamah, the soul the morning prayer calls pure. Your line was the soul is pure. Today, a list read every morning, of things with no ceiling.

Almost everything in a life of practice has a size. So many minutes of prayer. So many words in a blessing. A tenth of the harvest. Rules like that are a gift: you know when you've done it. But early in the morning service, many prayer books include a passage that goes the other way. It names a handful of things and says: these have no measure. It's a short list, and it starts in a farmer's field.
screen: `EVERYTHING HAS A SIZE.` → `YOU KNOW WHEN YOU'RE DONE.` → `THESE HAVE NO MEASURE.`

segments.voice: The passage is the opening of the Mishnah, tractate Peah: these are things that have no measure. First, peah, the corner of the field. The Torah tells farmers to leave the edges of their fields unharvested for the poor and the stranger, and never says how big the corner should be. Then the first fruits, and the pilgrim's offering at the Temple. Then gemilut chasadim, acts of loving-kindness. Then the study of Torah. The rabbis later set a minimum for the corner, one sixtieth of the field, and no maximum. Then the prayer book adds a second list, from the Talmud, tractate Shabbat: things whose fruit you enjoy in this life, while the principal stays for the world to come. Honoring your father and mother. Acts of kindness. Taking in guests. Visiting the sick. Helping a bride marry. Walking with the dead to their burial. Making peace between people. And it ends: the study of Torah is equal to them all; one reading says that's because study leads to doing. Why so early in the morning, close to the blessings for waking? One reading: the morning has just given thanks for eyes and legs and strength, and here's what they're for. The Jerusalem Talmud adds a careful note: giving money has limits, so you don't impoverish yourself, but kindness done with your own body, your time, your presence, has none.
screen: `MISHNAH PEAH: NO MEASURE.` · `THE CORNER OF THE FIELD.` · `FRUIT NOW, PRINCIPAL LATER.` · `MONEY HAS LIMITS; PRESENCE DOESN'T.` · then, large: `NO LIMIT ON KINDNESS.`

segments.voice: Let the list pass slowly: honoring a parent, a guest, someone sick, someone grieving, two people who aren't speaking. Notice which one brings a real name to mind, and stay with that person. Picture the smallest version of the deed: a call, a visit, a meal, a sentence that might make peace.
Peah. The corner of a field, left unharvested for the poor — one of the deeds the Mishnah says have no measure, no set size at all.
Your line: no limit on kindness. Money has limits; your time and presence don't. Day five hundred forty-seven, done.

howItsDone: Many prayer books place the Mishnah Peah passage and the list from tractate Shabbat right after the blessings over Torah study, so that each morning begins with a little learning about kindness.

fork.reveal: the Torah gives no size. the Mishnah lists peah first among things without measure; the rabbis set a minimum of one sixtieth, and no ceiling.

trapdoor: what you thought: a list of good deeds tacked onto the service.
what it means: right after thanking God for a working body, the morning names what that body is for, with no ceiling.
what a scholar hears: Mishnah Peah 1:1 and Shabbat 127a, placed after the Torah blessings as daily study; Jerusalem Talmud Peah 1:1 limits giving money but not personal kindness.

chat.says: How much kindness is enough? Is there a set amount, like with charity?
options: The Mishnah says kindness has no measure; money has limits, but your presence doesn't.
The rabbis set it at one sixtieth of your time, like the minimum for a field's corner.
Yes, a tenth of everything, and after that the obligation is fully finished.
chat.meaning: Mishnah Peah lists acts of loving-kindness among things with no measure; the Jerusalem Talmud limits giving money, but not kindness done with your own body.

Mishnah.meaning: the early rabbis' collection of Jewish law and teaching

Peah.meaning: the corner of the field, and the Mishnah tractate named for it

Jerusalem Talmud.meaning: the Talmud compiled in the Land of Israel

notes: Editor review (2026-10-01): 'because study is meant to lead to doing' was presented as the text's words; now marked as one reading (voice and myth reveal). The list's placement softened to 'so early, close to the blessings for waking' since order varies by rite. Added Mishnah Peah 1:2 as the source for the one-sixtieth minimum.
Mishnah Peah 1:1 list (peah, bikkurim, re'ayon, gemilut chasadim, Talmud Torah) paraphrased; confirm.

Second list from Shabbat 127a as found in the siddur: script names a selection (honoring parents, kindness, hospitality, visiting the sick, dowering the bride, escorting the dead, making peace); the siddur also includes early attendance at the study house and devotion in prayer. Confirm the selection is acceptable.
Minimum of one sixtieth for peah (Mishnah Peah 1:2); confirm.
Jerusalem Talmud Peah 1:1 distinction between giving money (limited, e.g. the Usha enactment of not more than a fifth) and kindness with one's body (unlimited); confirm.
'Study leads to doing' echoes Kiddushin 40b; not cited in the voice; confirm the gloss.
